realExample.text: Botswana used its diamond revenue to pay for roads, schools and clinics, and grew from one of the poorest countries at independence into an upper-middle-income economy.

sections.misconception: Students set primary industries against development. Many rich economies began with farming or mining; the question is whether the income is invested in diversifying the economy or captured by a few.
sections.examMatters: Say which constraint this strategy eases (foreign currency) and which it can worsen (volatility, the terms of trade); weighing the two for the country in the question is the evaluation.

recall.prompt: Match each primary-industry project to the development gain it aims for:

pairs.right: Two harvests a year instead of one for the poorest households
pairs.why: Most of the poor farm, so higher yields raise their incomes directly.

pairs.left: A copper refinery beside the mine
pairs.right: More of the metal's value earned inside the country
pairs.why: Processing adds value before export.

pairs.left: Cold stores at a fishing port
pairs.right: Catch sold later at a better price instead of spoiling
pairs.why: Storage cuts waste and steadies income.

pairs.left: A state fund built from oil revenue
pairs.right: Money for schools and roads after the wells run dry
pairs.why: Investing resource revenue diversifies the economy.

distractors: A rise in the price of imported cars

sections.title: Aid and Debt Relief
sections.keyIdea: Aid and debt relief add foreign resources a poor country lacks; whether they promote development depends on what they are spent on and the conditions attached.

body.text: **Aid** is the transfer of resources to a developing country on better terms than the market offers: grants, loans at low interest, food, equipment or expertise. It may come from one government or through institutions such as the World Bank. **Tied aid** must be spent on goods from the donor country.

In Harrod-Domar terms, aid fills the savings and foreign currency gaps. If Karanda invests aid worth 2% of GDP on top of its 12% saving, growth rises from 3% to 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5%. Humanitarian aid saves lives in a disaster; development aid can fund clinics, vaccination and schools directly.

**Debt relief** cancels or reduces a country's overseas debt, freeing the foreign currency and tax revenue that servicing absorbed. If Karanda's debt service fell from 15% to 5% of its $12bn export earnings, $1.2bn a year would be freed. Critics argue aid can create dependency, be captured by corrupt officials or serve the donor's interests, and that relief can reward past overborrowing.

realExample.text: Under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries initiative and the relief that followed it, more than 30 countries, most of them in Africa, had much of their overseas debt cancelled on condition that the savings went on reducing poverty.

sections.misconception: Students treat aid as either always good or always wasted. The evidence depends on the type: humanitarian aid and health programmes such as vaccination have clear effects, while large budget transfers to weak governments have much weaker ones.
sections.examMatters: When a question gives aid as a share of GDP, add it to domestic saving to show the Harrod-Domar effect, then evaluate with where the money goes and who controls it.

recall.prompt: Work out what aid and debt relief do for a different country:
template: It saves 8% of GDP with a capital-output ratio of 2, so it grows at ___ a year.
Aid worth 2% of GDP, all of it invested, lifts growth to ___ a year.
If debt service falls from 25% to 10% of $10bn of export earnings, $___bn a year is freed.
hints: the savings ratio divided by the capital-output ratio
saving plus aid, divided by the capital-output ratio
the fall in the share, times export earnings

sections.title: The World Bank and the IMF
sections.keyIdea: The World Bank lends for long-term development projects; the International Monetary Fund lends short-term to countries in balance of payments crisis, usually with conditions.

body.text: **The World Bank** is an international institution owned by its member governments. It lends for long-term development: roads, power, water, schools, health systems and reforms of how governments work. Its International Development Association gives grants and loans at very low interest to the poorest countries.

**The International Monetary Fund (IMF)** exists to keep the international monetary system stable. It lends to countries that cannot pay for their imports or debts — a balance of payments crisis, the foreign currency gap in its sharpest form — and it monitors and advises its members.

IMF loans usually come with **conditions**: cutting the budget deficit, removing subsidies, raising interest rates, letting the currency fall, privatising. Supporters argue the conditions fix the causes of the crisis and restore confidence, so private lenders and investors return. Critics argue they cut spending on health and education when the poor most need it, deepen recessions and impose one model on very different economies.

realExample.text: Pakistan and Sri Lanka have both turned to the IMF when they ran short of foreign currency; the loans came with conditions to raise tax revenue and cut energy subsidies.

sections.misconception: Students confuse the two institutions. The World Bank finances long-term development; the IMF lends short-term to countries in a balance of payments crisis. Both are owned by member governments and both lend with conditions.
sections.examMatters: The specification asks for their role (3d). An Evaluate on the IMF weighs the stability its loans restore against the social cost of its conditions, for the country in the question.

recall.prompt: Sort each activity into the World Bank's role or the IMF's role:

groups.name: The World Bank
items: A 30-year loan to build a hydroelectric dam
A grant to train rural health workers in the poorest countries
Finance for a new national road network
groups.why: Each is long-term finance for development projects.

groups.name: The IMF
items: An emergency loan to a country that cannot pay for its imports
A condition that the borrower cuts its budget deficit
A yearly check on a member economy's policies
groups.why: Each is about short-term stability: crisis lending, conditions and surveillance.

sections.title: Non-Government Organisations
sections.keyIdea: NGOs are independent, non-profit organisations that deliver aid and services directly to communities, often reaching people that governments and markets miss.

body.text: **Non-government organisations (NGOs)** are independent of governments and do not seek profit. They include international charities such as Oxfam and Médecins Sans Frontières and local organisations such as BRAC in Bangladesh. They are funded by donations, grants from governments and, sometimes, their own enterprises.

Their role in development: delivering emergency relief; running schools, clinics, clean-water and microfinance projects; training farmers; and campaigning, for example for debt relief. Working at community level, they can reach remote villages and target the poorest, often at lower cost and with less corruption than state programmes.

Their limits: they work on a small scale compared with governments; their funding is uncertain and can follow donors' priorities rather than local needs; many projects stop when the NGO leaves; and running services alongside the state can weaken it. They complement governments and the international institutions rather than replace them.

realExample.text: BRAC began as a small relief effort in Bangladesh and now runs schools, health programmes and microfinance serving millions of people across Asia and Africa.

sections.misconception: Students treat NGOs as the solution governments failed to find. Their strength is reach and targeting at small scale; national problems such as infrastructure or macroeconomic stability still need governments and institutions.
sections.examMatters: The role of NGOs is its own bullet in 3d. Compare them with the World Bank and the IMF on scale, targeting and accountability — that comparison is the evaluation an essay on institutions needs.

recall.prompt: Sort each statement into a strength or a limitation of NGOs in development:

groups.name: Strength
items: A charity health worker reaches a village with no road
Donations go straight to the families who lost their homes
A local group knows which households are poorest
groups.why: Each reflects reach and targeting at community level.

groups.name: Limitation
items: The water project stops when the grant runs out after three years
A donor's favourite cause gets funded before what villagers need
The charity runs ten clinics where the country needs a thousand
groups.why: Each reflects small scale, uncertain funding or donor-driven priorities.

takeaway: Lewis: surplus labour moves to industry until the turning point.
Tourism, primary industries, aid and debt relief each help and leak.
World Bank: long-term projects. IMF: crisis loans. NGOs: local reach.

notes.title: Measuring Development
notes.keyIdea: How development differs from growth, how the HDI is built and where it falls short, and the six other measures of development the specification names.

items.text: Economic development — an improvement in living standards and welfare: health, education, income and freedom, not output alone.
Human Development Index (HDI) — a composite index of health (life expectancy at birth), education (mean and expected years of schooling) and income (GNI per head at PPP).
Other measures — adult male labour in agriculture; access to clean water; energy consumption per capita; internet, mobile phones and doctors per thousand of population.
Geometric mean: a weak dimension pulls the index down more than an arithmetic mean would.
Measures of poverty and inequality within a country are topic 4.3.4.

takeaway: Growth helps pay for development; it does not guarantee it.
An average hides who gains; the data are weakest where it matters most.
Use single indicators alongside the HDI, not instead of it.

notes.title: Constraints: Commodities, Savings and Currency
notes.keyIdea: Five economic constraints that all come down to too little saving, too little foreign currency, or earnings that swing.

items.text: Prebisch-Singer hypothesis — primary product prices tend to fall relative to manufactures over time, so primary exporters' terms of trade decline.
Harrod-Domar model — growth = savings ratio ÷ capital-output ratio. The savings gap is the saving needed for a target growth rate minus actual saving.
Foreign currency gap — the foreign currency a growth plan needs minus what the country earns. Capital flight — residents moving their money abroad.
Copper 60% of exports × a 25% price fall = export earnings down 15%.
Terms of trade 90 ÷ 120 × 100 = 75. Harrod-Domar 12 ÷ 4 = 3%; 6% needs 24%: a gap of 12 points.
Exports $12bn against import needs of $14bn: a foreign currency gap of $2bn.

takeaway: Volatility, not only low prices, makes planning impossible.
Harrod-Domar points to foreign savings to fill the gap.
Capital flight drains savings and foreign currency at once.

notes.title: Constraints: People, Debt, Credit and Infrastructure
notes.keyIdea: Five constraints on the people, the finance and the physical capital an economy needs to grow.

items.text: Dependency ratio — people under 15 and over 64 per 100 of working age.
Household debt — what families owe; overseas debt — what a country owes abroad, serviced in foreign currency.
Access to credit and banking — whether people can save safely and borrow for productive projects.
Karanda: (42 + 4) ÷ 54 × 100 = 85 dependants per hundred.
Debt service $1.8bn = 15% of export earnings, gone before any import is bought.
No collateral, no loan, no machine: the savings gap seen from below.

takeaway: Fast population growth eats the rise in output.
Debt constrains when its cost exceeds what it produced.
Missing infrastructure and skills raise every cost.

notes.title: Non-Economic Constraints
notes.keyIdea: Corruption, poor governance, civil wars, migration and terrorism: constraints that are not economic in origin but act through investment and capacity.

items.text: Corruption — abuse of public office for private gain. Poor governance — the state failing to provide reliable rules, courts and policy.
Brain drain — emigration of skilled workers. Remittances — money migrants send home.
Corruption: a hidden tax on investment, and production inside the frontier.
Civil war: capital destroyed and workers lost — the frontier shifts inward.
Migration also appears as a demographic factor in 2a.

takeaway: Name the mechanism, not just the moral point.
War shrinks capacity; corruption wastes it.
Migration both costs and returns resources.

notes.title: Market-Orientated Strategies
notes.keyIdea: Six market-orientated strategies: open trade, attract investment, withdraw subsidies and state ownership, let the currency float, and bring credit to the poor.

items.text: Trade liberalisation — removing barriers to trade. FDI — a foreign firm investing in productive assets it controls.
Privatisation — selling state-owned firms to private owners. Floating exchange rate — a value set by the market.
Microfinance — small loans and savings for people banks will not serve, often through groups.
FDI of 6% plus saving of 12%: growth 3% → 4.5%.
Falling export earnings → depreciation → cheaper exports, with no reserves spent.
How trade barriers work is 4.3.2; exchange rate systems as such are 4.3.3.

takeaway: Each strategy answers a named constraint.
Gains depend on links to local firms and on competition.
The costs fall on identifiable groups.

notes.title: Interventionist Strategies
notes.keyIdea: Six interventionist strategies: invest in people and infrastructure, protect and steer, and stabilise commodity prices.

items.text: Human capital — the skills, knowledge and health that make people productive.
Managed exchange rate — market-set but steered by the central bank. Joint venture — a TNC and a local partner sharing ownership.
Buffer stock scheme — buying at a floor price and selling at a ceiling price to hold the price in a band.
Coffee: bumper harvest of 480k tonnes → $1.60; the agency buys 80k tonnes to hold $2.00.
Poor harvest of 300k tonnes → $2.50; the agency sells 20k tonnes to hold $2.40.
Infant industry: protection buys time to cut costs, if it is temporary.

takeaway: Intervention fills gaps markets leave.
Every scheme needs money, reserves or time.
Temporary and targeted beats permanent and general.

notes.title: Other Strategies and International Institutions
notes.keyIdea: Industrialisation through the Lewis model, tourism, primary industries, aid and debt relief — and the World Bank, the IMF and NGOs.

items.text: Lewis dual-sector model — surplus labour moves from traditional farming to a modern sector until the turning point.
Aid — resources on better-than-market terms. Debt relief — cancelling or reducing overseas debt.
World Bank — long-term development finance. IMF — short-term crisis lending with conditions. NGOs — independent non-profits.
Lewis: a wage of $3 against $2 on the farm; jobs grow 2 → 3 → 4 million until the turning point at 5 million.
Aid of 2%: growth 3% → 3.5%. Debt relief 15% → 5%: $1.2bn freed.
Tourism and primary industries share the commodity exporter's volatility.

takeaway: Lewis depends on reinvested profits and jobs for migrants.
Aid and relief work where the money reaches services.
The institutions differ in time scale, conditions and reach.

quiz.question: Which of these is one of the three components of the Human Development Index?
options: the unemployment rate
life expectancy at birth
the inflation rate
the budget balance
quiz.explanation: The HDI combines health, measured by life expectancy at birth, with education and income. Unemployment, inflation and the budget balance are measures of macroeconomic performance, not of human development.

quiz.question: Economic development differs from economic growth because development:
options: covers health and education, not just output
measures only the rise in real GDP
happens only in high-income economies
is measured at current prices
quiz.explanation: Growth is a rise in real output. Development is a rise in the quality of people's lives — longer lives, more schooling, higher incomes shared more widely — which growth can help pay for but does not guarantee.

quiz.question: The HDI combines its three dimension indices by taking:
options: their simple sum
their geometric mean
the highest of the three
their ratio to GDP
quiz.explanation: The HDI is the cube root of the product of the three indices. A geometric mean means a very weak dimension pulls the index down more than it would in an ordinary average.

quiz.question: A country's life expectancy at birth is 50 years. Using HDI goalposts of 20 and 85 years, its health index is:
quiz.explanation: The index is the distance above the minimum as a share of the whole range: (50 − 20) ÷ (85 − 20) = 30 ÷ 65 = 0.462. Dividing 50 by 85, or by 65, ignores the minimum goalpost.

quiz.question: Why does the HDI use a geometric rather than an arithmetic mean?
options: it gives income twice the weight of health
it is simpler to calculate by hand
it removes the need for goalposts
a very low score in one dimension pulls it down more
quiz.explanation: With a geometric mean, high income cannot make up for very short lives. An arithmetic mean would let a strong dimension hide a weak one; the goalposts are still needed to scale each dimension beforehand.

quiz.question: Which is a limitation of the HDI when comparing living standards between countries?
options: it measures income alone
it is an average that hides how evenly gains are shared
it cannot be calculated for developing countries
it ignores life expectancy
quiz.explanation: A national average can rise because the better-off gain while the poorest do not. The HDI measures three dimensions, not income alone, and life expectancy is one of them.

quiz.question: A high percentage of adult male labour in agriculture suggests an economy that:
options: has a highly mechanised farm sector
has not yet shifted much into industry and services
uses a great deal of energy per capita
has many doctors per thousand of population
quiz.explanation: Output per worker is usually far higher in industry and services, so a large share of men working the land shows the structural shift that comes with development has not gone far.

quiz.question: Growth without development is most likely when:
options: life expectancy and schooling both rise
the income from growth goes mainly to a small elite
real GDP falls for two years in a row
the HDI rises faster than GDP
quiz.explanation: If extra income is captured by a few, output can rise while health, schooling and most people's incomes barely change. Rising life expectancy and schooling are development.

quiz.question: Copper is 50% of a country's export earnings and its world price falls by 20%. Export earnings fall by:
quiz.explanation: The fall in earnings is the good's share of exports times the fall in its price: 0.5 × 20% = 10%. Using the price fall alone assumes copper is all the country exports.

quiz.question: The Prebisch-Singer hypothesis predicts that, over the long run, the terms of trade of primary product exporters will:
options: improve
stay constant
decline
double
quiz.explanation: Primary product prices tend to fall relative to manufactures, so each unit of exports buys fewer imports: the terms of trade decline.

quiz.question: One reason given for the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis is that demand for primary products is:
options: income inelastic
price elastic
income elastic
perfectly elastic
quiz.explanation: As world incomes rise, spending on food and raw materials rises more slowly than spending on manufactures and services, so primary prices lag behind.

quiz.question: In the Harrod-Domar model, a country saving 20% of GDP with a capital-output ratio of 5 grows at:
quiz.explanation: Growth = savings ratio ÷ capital-output ratio = 20 ÷ 5 = 4%. Multiplying the two, or subtracting one from the other, has no meaning in the model.

quiz.question: A foreign currency gap exists when:
options: export earnings fall short of the imports growth needs
domestic saving is below the investment needed
the government spends more than it collects in tax
imports are smaller than exports
quiz.explanation: The gap is a shortage of foreign currency to pay for imports such as machinery and fuel. Too little domestic saving is the savings gap, a different constraint.

quiz.question: Capital flight is best described as:
options: foreign aid being withdrawn by donors
residents moving their savings out of the country
a fall in the price of capital goods
machinery wearing out faster than it is replaced
quiz.explanation: Capital flight is money moved abroad by a country's own residents and firms, usually out of fear for its safety at home. It drains both domestic savings and foreign currency.

quiz.question: An emerging economy's birth rate has fallen: 20% of its people are under 15 and 5% are over 64. Its dependency ratio is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Working age is what is left: 100 − 20 − 5 = 75%. The dependency ratio is (young + old) ÷ working age × 100 = 25 ÷ 75 × 100 = 33. Taking working age as 80% forgets to take out the over-64s and gives 31; leaving the over-64s out of the dependants gives 27; dividing the whole population by the working age gives 133.

quiz.question: Overseas debt constrains development mainly because servicing it:
options: raises the savings ratio at home
lowers the capital-output ratio
increases the country's export earnings
uses up foreign currency and tax revenue
quiz.explanation: Interest and repayments are paid in foreign currency, often from tax revenue, before any imports or public services are paid for.

quiz.question: Why do small farmers in many developing economies find it hard to borrow from banks?
options: interest rates are set at zero
banks may lend only to exporters
they have no collateral such as a land title
their incomes are too high to qualify
quiz.explanation: Without a land title or formal records, a farmer has nothing a bank can lend against, so many turn to moneylenders at very high interest.

quiz.question: Unreliable electricity supply constrains growth mainly because it:
options: lowers the price of imported fuel
increases the dependency ratio
raises the savings ratio
raises firms' costs and interrupts production
quiz.explanation: Firms must stop work or run their own generators, which raises costs at every level of output and deters investment, including FDI.

quiz.question: Low levels of education and skills constrain growth mainly by:
options: raising the savings ratio
increasing export prices
keeping output per worker low
reducing the population
quiz.explanation: A workforce with little schooling produces little per worker and cannot run or repair modern equipment, so incomes and investment stay low.

quiz.question: Corruption constrains investment mainly because it:
options: lowers the tax rate on profits
makes contracts easier to enforce
increases the supply of credit
raises the cost and risk of investing
quiz.explanation: Bribes and unreliable decisions act like a tax on investment: a firm needs a higher expected return before it invests, so less is invested.

quiz.question: Which is an example of poor governance rather than corruption?
options: an official demanding a bribe for a licence
courts taking years to settle a contract dispute
a contract given to a minister's relative
customs officers taking cash to let goods through
quiz.explanation: Slow courts are a failure of the state to provide reliable rules; nobody need be taking a bribe. The other three are abuses of public office for private gain.

quiz.question: On a production possibility frontier, a civil war that destroys factories and roads is best shown as:
options: an inward shift of the frontier
a movement along the frontier
an outward shift of the frontier
a point beyond the frontier
quiz.explanation: Capital and workers are lost, so the economy can produce less of everything: its frontier shifts inward.

quiz.question: The loss of doctors who emigrate from a developing country is partly offset when emigrants:
options: raise the dependency ratio
reduce the country's exports
send remittances home in foreign currency
widen the savings gap
quiz.explanation: Remittances raise household incomes and ease the foreign currency gap, which is why emigration is weighed, not simply counted as a loss.

quiz.question: Terrorism reduces growth in the regions it affects mainly by:
options: deterring investors and tourists
raising the price of exports abroad
increasing the number of doctors
lowering the dependency ratio
quiz.explanation: Fear keeps people at home and keeps investors and tourists away, and firms pay for security; the damage is concentrated where the attacks happen.

quiz.question: Trade liberalisation is most likely to narrow a developing economy's foreign currency gap by:
options: reducing imports of machinery and fuel
raising import duties on manufactures
raising export earnings as firms reach larger markets
banning foreign ownership of firms
quiz.explanation: Open markets let exporters sell more abroad, which earns the foreign currency that pays for imports. Raising duties and banning foreign ownership are the opposite of liberalisation.

quiz.question: A country saves 11% of GDP and receives FDI of 4% of GDP. With a capital-output ratio of 3, Harrod-Domar predicts growth of:
quiz.explanation: Investment is domestic saving plus FDI: 11% + 4% = 15% of GDP. Growth = 15 ÷ 3 = 5%. Using saving alone gives 3.7%, and multiplying gives 45%.

quiz.question: Which is a likely cost of promoting FDI for the host country?
options: domestic investment rises
technology is transferred to local firms
profits are repatriated to the parent company
export markets become accessible
quiz.explanation: Part of the income from FDI flows back to the foreign owner. The other three are benefits the strategy aims for.

quiz.question: Removing a fuel subsidy is most likely to:
options: lower the price of fuel for households
increase the budget deficit
free government revenue but raise transport costs
reduce the price of food
quiz.explanation: The government stops paying to hold the price down, so it saves money, and the price households and firms pay rises to its true cost.

quiz.question: Under a floating exchange rate, a fall in a country's export earnings will tend to:
options: appreciate its currency, making imports cheaper
leave the exchange rate unchanged
depreciate its currency, making exports cheaper
use up the central bank's reserves
quiz.explanation: Less demand for the currency lowers its market value. No reserves are spent, because the central bank is not defending a target.

quiz.question: Microfinance schemes often lend to groups of borrowers because:
options: members guarantee each other in place of collateral
groups qualify for lower tax rates
banks are required to lend to groups
groups can borrow in foreign currency
quiz.explanation: Poor borrowers have no collateral, so the group's joint responsibility for repayment takes its place, and members check on each other.

quiz.question: The infant industry argument for protection says a new industry needs shelter because:
options: it can never match imports on cost
it pays no tax
consumers prefer imported goods
its costs are high until it grows and learns
quiz.explanation: A new industry is small and inexperienced, so its costs start high. Temporary protection gives it time to grow and cut them; the argument fails if it can never compete.

quiz.question: A central bank sells its dollar reserves to buy its own currency. It is trying to:
options: make its exports cheaper
stop its currency falling
increase its reserves
raise the money supply
quiz.explanation: Buying its own currency raises demand for it and holds its value up, which uses reserves.

quiz.question: A coffee buffer stock has a floor of $2 a kilogram. A bumper harvest would push the price to $1.50. The agency will:
options: buy coffee to hold the price at the floor
sell coffee from its stock
do nothing, as the price is inside the band
raise the ceiling price
quiz.explanation: Below the floor, the agency buys the surplus that buyers do not want at the floor price, so the market price stays at the floor.

quiz.question: Why do governments, rather than private firms, build most infrastructure in developing economies?
options: it pays back slowly and benefits many who do not pay
private firms are not allowed to build roads
infrastructure brings no benefit to anyone
governments pay lower wages
quiz.explanation: Infrastructure is costly, lasts decades and its benefits spread to people who do not pay for them, so private firms build too little of it.

quiz.question: In a joint venture between a TNC and a local firm, the host country gains mainly because:
options: the TNC pays no tax
imports of machinery are banned
the currency stops moving
local partners share profits and technology
quiz.explanation: Shared ownership keeps part of the profit in the country, and working alongside the TNC transfers technology and management methods.

quiz.question: Developing human capital raises growth mainly by:
options: raising the dependency ratio
reducing export earnings
lowering the savings ratio
increasing output per worker
quiz.explanation: Education, training and health make each worker more productive, and attract investors who need trained staff — with a long delay before the effect arrives.

quiz.question: In the Lewis dual-sector model, surplus labour refers to farm workers whose:
options: wages are above factory wages
extra output is close to zero
jobs are in the modern sector
skills are in short supply
quiz.explanation: There are so many workers on the land that removing some barely reduces the harvest, so they can move to the modern sector at almost no cost to farm output.

quiz.question: In the Lewis model, the modern sector keeps expanding because:
options: the government sets a minimum wage
its profits are reinvested in more capital
farm output rises each year
workers return to the farms
quiz.explanation: High profits, reinvested, grow the capital stock, which raises the modern sector's demand for workers at an unchanged wage.

quiz.question: The Lewis turning point is reached when:
options: surplus labour runs out and wages start to rise
the traditional sector grows faster than industry
profits are no longer reinvested
all workers leave the modern sector
quiz.explanation: While surplus labour lasts, the modern sector can hire at a constant wage. Once it is used up, it must bid workers away from farming, so wages rise.

quiz.question: Tourism earnings leak abroad when visitors:
options: hire local guides for safari trips
pay the government's airport tax on departure
stay in foreign-owned hotels and eat imported food
buy fruit grown on nearby farms at market
quiz.explanation: Money paid to foreign owners and suppliers leaves the country. Wages for local guides, taxes and purchases from local farms stay.

quiz.question: The IMF differs from the World Bank mainly because the IMF:
options: lends short-term to countries in balance of payments crises
finances long-term projects such as dams
is owned by private shareholders
lends only to developed economies
quiz.explanation: The IMF provides crisis lending with conditions; the World Bank lends for long-term development projects. Both are owned by member governments.

quiz.question: Debt relief promotes development mainly by:
options: raising the country's interest rates
increasing its overseas borrowing
freeing money that went on servicing debt
lowering its export earnings
quiz.explanation: Cancelled debt no longer absorbs foreign currency and tax revenue, which can then pay for imports, health and schooling.

quiz.question: A strength of NGOs in delivering development projects is that they:
options: operate on a far larger scale than governments
can set a country's interest rates
lend to countries in currency crises
can reach and target the poorest communities directly
quiz.explanation: Working at community level, NGOs can reach remote villages and target the poorest. Their scale is small, and crisis lending is the IMF's role.

quiz.question: Developing primary industries risks worsening which constraint?
options: a shortage of surplus labour
a low dependency ratio
dependence on volatile commodity prices
too much foreign currency
quiz.explanation: More reliance on crops and minerals exposes export earnings to swings in their world prices and, on the Prebisch-Singer argument, to declining terms of trade.

practice.question: Define the term 'Human Development Index'. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two marks means two separate points. Decide what kind of measure the HDI is, and then what goes into it — listing the parts without saying they are combined into one index is only half an answer.
The HDI is a composite index of human development, published by the United Nations (1 mark), that combines three dimensions: health, measured by life expectancy at birth; education, measured by mean and expected years of schooling; and income, measured by GNI per head at purchasing power parity (1 mark). "Health, education and wealth" does not earn the second mark: the third dimension is income.

practice.question: A country's life expectancy at birth is 66 years. Calculate its HDI health index, using the goalposts of 20 and 85 years. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Calculate asks for the working as well as the answer (Appendix 6). Before any arithmetic, decide where the country sits between the two goalposts — the index is the distance above the minimum as a share of the whole range.
Health index = (actual − minimum) ÷ (maximum − minimum) = (66 − 20) ÷ (85 − 20) = 46 ÷ 65 (1 mark) = 0.708 (1 mark). Dividing 66 by 85 ignores the minimum goalpost.

practice.question: Explain how dependence on primary products can constrain a developing economy's growth, with reference to the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants linked stages for an Explain. Start from what happens to the prices of primary products relative to manufactures over time, and carry the chain through to what the country can afford to import.
Knowledge: the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis states that the prices of primary products tend to fall over time relative to the prices of manufactured goods (1 mark). Reason: demand for primary products is income inelastic, so as world incomes rise spending on them grows more slowly (1 mark). Analysis: the terms of trade of a primary exporter therefore decline, so each unit of exports buys fewer imports (1 mark). Analysis: machinery and other capital goods cost more exports, so investment and growth are constrained (1 mark).

practice.question: A country saves 20% of its GDP and has a capital-output ratio of 5. Its population grows by 2.5% a year. Calculate, using the Harrod-Domar model, its annual rate of growth of GDP and of GDP per head. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Calculate asks for workings (Appendix 6). Write down the model's equation before substituting anything, and read the question again for the second figure it asks for: growth of GDP and growth per head are different answers.
Growth = savings ratio ÷ capital-output ratio = 20% ÷ 5 (1 mark) = 4% a year (1 mark). Growth of GDP per head ≈ growth of GDP − population growth = 4% − 2.5% (1 mark) = 1.5% a year (1 mark). Multiplying 20 by 5 instead of dividing is the common error.

practice.question: Analyse how a high dependency ratio may constrain growth and development in a developing economy. (6 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants depth for an Analyse: one route followed through several linked stages. Decide first which dependants the question means — a young population and an ageing one constrain through different channels.
Knowledge: the dependency ratio is the number of people under 15 and over 64 for every 100 of working age (1 mark). Application: in a young, fast-growing population a large share of income goes on feeding and schooling children (1 mark). Analysis, first stage: households have little left to save, so savings available for investment are low (1 mark). Analysis, second stage: in the Harrod-Domar model, lower saving means lower investment and slower growth (1 mark). Analysis, third stage: the government must fund school places and clinics for a rising number of children, leaving less for infrastructure (1 mark). Development: income per head grows slowly when population growth absorbs most of the rise in output (1 mark).

practice.question: Examine the impact of corruption and poor governance on growth and development in developing economies. (8 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants a chain of reasoning and a brief assessment for an Examine, so save room for a judgement. Separate the two factors before writing: taking bribes is not the same failure as courts that cannot enforce a contract.
Level 1 states that corruption harms growth, with little explanation. Level 2 explains a chain: bribes and unreliable courts raise the cost and risk of investing, so less is invested and growth slows. Level 3 develops two chains with application — public money diverted from roads and clinics, so development suffers directly; foreign investors choosing other countries, so the savings and foreign currency gaps stay open. The brief assessment that lifts an answer to the top of the range weighs how much it matters: some economies have grown fast despite corruption, and its effect depends on whether it is predictable or arbitrary and on how much investment it touches.

practice.question: Discuss the likely impact of trade liberalisation on growth and development in a developing economy. (14 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and a critical assessment. Plan the case for and the case against before writing, and decide what your judgement will depend on — the kind of goods the economy exports is the obvious place to start.
Level 1 describes liberalisation with little explanation. Level 2 explains one side: larger export markets and cheaper imported inputs raise export earnings and investment, narrowing the foreign currency gap. Level 3 develops both sides with application: for it, specialisation, competition and cheaper capital goods; against it, infant industries wiped out by established rivals, deeper dependence on primary products and declining terms of trade, lost revenue from import duties, and workers in closing industries. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement that follows from the argument: liberalisation tends to help an economy with manufacturing capacity and diversified exports more than one that exports a single commodity, and it works best phased in, with support for the industries and workers that lose out.

practice.question: Evaluate the view that interventionist strategies are more effective than market-orientated strategies in promoting growth and development in developing economies. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants multi-stage chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and informed judgements. Plan the strongest case for each approach before writing, and decide in advance what your judgement will turn on, so that the conclusion follows from the argument rather than appearing at the end.
Level 1 lists strategies with little explanation. Level 2 explains how one or two strategies work — for example, human capital raising output per worker, or FDI adding to investment. Level 3 develops both approaches with chains and application: interventionist strategies fill gaps markets leave (infrastructure, schooling, stable commodity prices) but need money, reserves and honest administration; market-orientated strategies raise efficiency and draw in foreign savings but can deepen inequality and dependence on primary products. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: the most defensible is conditional — interventionist strategies are strongest where markets are missing and the state is capable, market-orientated ones where markets function and governance is weak, and most successful developing economies combined the two, protecting and investing while pushing firms to export.

practice.question: Evaluate the extent to which industrialisation, as described by the Lewis dual-sector model, can promote development in a developing economy. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants multi-stage chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and informed judgements. Start from what the model assumes, because every strong evaluation of it tests those assumptions against the economy in the question.
Level 1 describes industrialisation with little explanation. Level 2 explains the model: surplus labour in traditional farming moves to a modern sector paying a wage just above farm incomes, and reinvested profits keep creating jobs. Level 3 develops the process and its limits: output per worker rises as labour moves, incomes and tax revenue grow, and the turning point raises wages; against that, profits may be sent abroad or spent, factories may use labour-saving machines, and migrants can arrive in cities faster than jobs, leaving unemployment and slums. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: industrialisation promotes development where profits are reinvested, industry is labour-intensive and workers have the skills to move — conditions that depend on human capital, infrastructure and governance as much as on the model itself.

practice.question: Evaluate the role of the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and non-government organisations in promoting growth and development. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants multi-stage chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and informed judgements. The three institutions do different jobs, so plan what each is for before judging how well it does it.
Level 1 describes one institution with little explanation. Level 2 explains their roles: the World Bank finances long-term development projects; the IMF lends short-term to countries in balance of payments crises; NGOs deliver aid and services directly to communities. Level 3 develops their effects on both sides: World Bank projects build infrastructure and human capital but can add to debt and suit donors' priorities; IMF loans restore stability and confidence but their conditions can cut health and education spending and deepen recessions; NGOs reach the poorest at low cost but on a small scale and with uncertain funding. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: their contributions complement one another, and their effectiveness depends on the country's governance and on whether conditions and projects fit its circumstances.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between economic growth and economic development?
flashcards.back: Growth is a rise in real GDP. Development is a rise in the quality of people's lives — health, education, income shared widely — which growth can help pay for but does not guarantee.

flashcards.front: Name the three components of the HDI and their indicators.
flashcards.back: Health: life expectancy at birth. Education: mean and expected years of schooling. Income: GNI per head at purchasing power parity.

flashcards.front: How is a dimension index calculated for the HDI?
flashcards.back: (Actual − minimum goalpost) ÷ (maximum − minimum). For health the goalposts are 20 and 85 years.

flashcards.front: How are the three HDI indices combined?
flashcards.back: By a geometric mean: the cube root of their product. A very weak dimension pulls the index down more than an arithmetic mean would.

flashcards.front: Give two advantages of the HDI for comparing living standards.
flashcards.back: It goes beyond income, and it puts every country on the same 0-to-1 scale that can be tracked over time.

flashcards.front: Give three limitations of the HDI.
flashcards.back: It is an average that hides inequality; it leaves out freedom, safety and the quality of schooling; its data are weakest in the poorest countries.

flashcards.front: Name the six other measures of development in the specification.
flashcards.back: Adult male labour in agriculture; access to clean water; energy consumption per capita; internet, mobile phones and doctors per thousand of population.

flashcards.front: What does a high share of adult male labour in agriculture suggest?
flashcards.back: The economy has not shifted far from farming into industry and services, where output per worker is higher.

flashcards.front: Why is commodity price volatility a constraint?
flashcards.back: Export earnings, tax revenue and incomes swing with world prices, so investment is postponed and planning is hard.

flashcards.front: How do you estimate the fall in export earnings from a commodity price fall?
flashcards.back: Multiply the commodity's share of export earnings by the fall in its price: 60% × 25% = 15%.

flashcards.front: State the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis.
flashcards.back: Over the long run the prices of primary products tend to fall relative to manufactures, so primary exporters' terms of trade decline.

flashcards.front: Why might primary product prices fall relative to manufactures?
flashcards.back: Demand for primary products is income inelastic, and manufacturers turn productivity gains into profits and wages rather than lower prices.

flashcards.front: State the Harrod-Domar growth equation.
flashcards.back: Growth rate = savings ratio ÷ capital-output ratio. Saving 12% with a ratio of 4 gives 3% growth.

flashcards.front: What is the savings gap?
flashcards.back: The saving needed for a target growth rate minus actual saving. Growth of 6% at a ratio of 4 needs 24%; saving 12% leaves a gap of 12 points.

flashcards.front: Give two criticisms of the Harrod-Domar model.
flashcards.back: It assumes a fixed capital-output ratio, and that savings are invested productively; capital without skills or lost to corruption adds little output.

flashcards.front: What is the foreign currency gap?
flashcards.back: The shortfall between the foreign currency a growth plan needs for imports and debt payments and what the country earns from exports.

flashcards.front: What is capital flight and why does it constrain growth?
flashcards.back: Residents moving their money abroad. It drains domestic savings and foreign currency, widening both gaps.

flashcards.front: How is the dependency ratio calculated?
flashcards.back: (People under 15 + people over 64) ÷ people of working age × 100.

flashcards.front: How does a high dependency ratio constrain development?
flashcards.back: Each worker supports more dependants, so less is saved, and public money goes on school places rather than investment.

flashcards.front: Distinguish household debt from overseas debt.
flashcards.back: Household debt is what families owe, often to moneylenders. Overseas debt is what a country owes abroad and must service in foreign currency.

flashcards.front: Why does a lack of access to credit and banking constrain growth?
flashcards.back: Savings sit idle as cash or livestock, and small firms with no collateral cannot borrow to invest.

flashcards.front: How does poor infrastructure constrain growth?
flashcards.back: Unreliable power, poor roads and congested ports raise every firm's costs, cut people off from markets and deter FDI.

flashcards.front: Distinguish corruption from poor governance.
flashcards.back: Corruption is abuse of public office for private gain. Poor governance is the state failing to provide reliable rules, courts and policy.

flashcards.front: How does a civil war appear on a production possibility frontier?
flashcards.back: As an inward shift: capital is destroyed and workers are killed or flee, so less of everything can be produced.

flashcards.front: Give one cost and one benefit of emigration for a developing country.
flashcards.back: Cost: skilled workers lost (brain drain). Benefit: remittances sent home in foreign currency.

flashcards.front: Name the six market-orientated strategies in the specification.
flashcards.back: Trade liberalisation, promotion of FDI, removal of government subsidies, privatisation, floating exchange rate systems, microfinance schemes.

flashcards.front: How does FDI affect growth in the Harrod-Domar model?
flashcards.back: It adds foreign savings to domestic saving. Saving 12% plus FDI of 6% raises investment to 18% and growth from 3% to 4.5% at a ratio of 4.

flashcards.front: Give one argument for and one against removing a fuel subsidy.
flashcards.back: For: it frees government revenue for health and schools. Against: transport and food costs rise sharply for the poor.

flashcards.front: How does microfinance lend without collateral?
flashcards.back: Through groups whose members guarantee each other's repayment.

flashcards.front: Name the six interventionist strategies in the specification.
flashcards.back: Development of human capital, protectionism, managed exchange rates, infrastructure development, promoting joint ventures with TNCs, buffer stock schemes.

flashcards.front: What is the infant industry argument?
flashcards.back: A new industry has high costs until it grows and learns, so it needs temporary protection from established foreign rivals.

flashcards.front: How does a buffer stock scheme work?
flashcards.back: An agency buys the commodity when its price falls to a floor and sells from store when it rises to a ceiling.

flashcards.front: Why do buffer stock schemes often fail?
flashcards.back: A floor set too high means the agency keeps buying until its money runs out; perishable goods cannot be stored.

flashcards.front: What is a joint venture with a TNC?
flashcards.back: A foreign firm producing in partnership with a local firm or the state, sharing ownership, profits and decisions.

flashcards.front: Name the other strategies listed in 3c.
flashcards.back: Industrialisation (the Lewis model), development of tourism, development of primary industries, debt relief and aid.

flashcards.front: Summarise the Lewis dual-sector model.
flashcards.back: Surplus labour moves from traditional farming to a modern sector at a wage just above farm incomes; reinvested profits create more jobs until the turning point.

flashcards.front: What is the Lewis turning point?
flashcards.back: The point at which surplus labour is used up, so the modern sector must raise wages to attract more workers.

flashcards.front: What are tourism leakages?
flashcards.back: Tourist spending that goes to foreign owners and suppliers — foreign hotel chains, airlines, imported food — rather than staying in the host economy.

flashcards.front: What is tied aid?
flashcards.back: Aid that must be spent on goods and services from the donor country.

flashcards.front: What does debt relief free up?
flashcards.back: The foreign currency and tax revenue that servicing overseas debt used to absorb.

flashcards.front: What is the role of the World Bank?
flashcards.back: To lend for long-term development — infrastructure, schools, health — with grants and very cheap loans to the poorest countries.

flashcards.front: What is the role of the IMF?
flashcards.back: To keep the international monetary system stable, lending short-term with conditions to countries in balance of payments crises.

flashcards.front: What are NGOs and what is their role?
flashcards.back: Independent non-profit organisations that deliver aid and services directly to communities and campaign for change.

mistakes.title: Treating growth and development as the same thing
mistakes.looks_like: "Real GDP rose 6%, so the country has developed."
mistakes.why: A rise in output says nothing about who received it or whether lives got longer and healthier. If the gains go to a few, output rises while development barely moves.
mistakes.instead: Say what happened to health, schooling and the spread of income as well as to output, and use the HDI or another indicator to show it.

mistakes.title: Calling the HDI's third dimension "wealth"
mistakes.looks_like: "The HDI measures health, education and wealth."
mistakes.why: The third dimension is income: GNI per head at purchasing power parity, on a log scale. Wealth is a stock of assets and is not in the index.
mistakes.instead: Name all three indicators: life expectancy at birth; mean and expected years of schooling; GNI per head at PPP.

mistakes.title: Listing HDI limitations without tying them to the comparison
mistakes.looks_like: "The HDI ignores inequality, freedom and the environment."
mistakes.why: A list is description. The question asks how well the HDI compares living standards, so each limitation needs a consequence for that comparison.
mistakes.instead: Say which comparison the limitation distorts — between countries, the averaging and the data; over time, changes in the method — and how.

mistakes.title: Multiplying instead of dividing in Harrod-Domar
mistakes.looks_like: "Saving 20% with a capital-output ratio of 5 gives growth of 100%."
mistakes.why: The model divides: growth is the savings ratio over the capital-output ratio, so 20 ÷ 5 = 4%. A higher capital-output ratio means capital is less productive, which lowers growth.
mistakes.instead: Write g = s ÷ k before substituting, and check that a larger capital-output ratio gives a smaller growth rate.

mistakes.title: Confusing the savings gap with the foreign currency gap
mistakes.looks_like: "The country lacks money for investment, which is the foreign currency gap."
mistakes.why: The savings gap is too little saving at home; the foreign currency gap is too little foreign currency for imports. A country can have enough of one and too little of the other.
mistakes.instead: Name which gap, and the import or the investment it blocks. Say which source — FDI, aid, borrowing or exports — would fill it.

mistakes.title: Evaluating a strategy without naming the constraint it addresses
mistakes.looks_like: "Microfinance is good because it helps the poor."
mistakes.why: Every strategy in 3a-3d answers one or more constraints in 2a-2b. Without the link, the answer cannot say when the strategy will work.
mistakes.instead: Pair each strategy with its constraint — microfinance with access to credit, FDI with the savings gap — then judge whether it fits the country in the question.

mistakes.title: Confusing the World Bank with the IMF
mistakes.looks_like: "The World Bank lends to countries in a currency crisis."
mistakes.why: Crisis lending to countries that cannot pay for their imports is the IMF's role. The World Bank finances long-term development projects.
mistakes.instead: World Bank: long-term projects. IMF: short-term balance of payments support with conditions. NGOs: local delivery.

diagrams.description: IAL 4.3.6 · 2a: primary exporters' terms of trade declining (Prebisch-Singer), the Harrod-Domar savings gap, and the foreign currency gap, all for one economy.

chains.title: From a copper price fall to slower growth
steps: The world copper price falls 25%. Copper is 60% of Karanda's export earnings.
Export earnings fall by 60% × 25% = 15%: $1.8bn of $12bn.
With less foreign currency, the foreign currency gap of $2bn widens.
Tax revenue from the mines falls, and the government postpones roads and schools.
Firms cannot import the machinery they planned to buy, so investment and growth fall.
chains.result: A commodity price fall hits growth through export earnings, tax revenue and foreign currency at once — which is why volatility of commodity prices is the first economic constraint the specification lists.

chains.title: The Harrod-Domar savings gap, in figures
steps: Karanda saves 12% of GDP; its capital-output ratio is 4.
Growth = 12 ÷ 4 = 3%. Population grows 2.5%, so income per head rises about 0.5%.
A target of 6% needs saving of 6 × 4 = 24%: a gap of 12 points, $7.2bn a year.
FDI of 6% raises growth to 4.5%; aid of 2%, invested, to 3.5%.
Capital flight of 2% of GDP costs 0.5 points of growth a year.
chains.result: The model turns every constraint and strategy on saving and investment into a growth figure. Its weakness is the assumption that the capital-output ratio stays fixed — capital without skills, infrastructure or honest management is far less productive.

chains.title: The Lewis process, stage by stage
steps: Traditional farming holds surplus labour: workers whose extra output is close to zero.
The modern sector offers $3 a day against $2 on the farm, and workers migrate.
Its profits are high; reinvested, they add capital and create more jobs at the same wage.
Employment grows from 2 to 4 million as the process repeats.
At 5 million the surplus is gone: the turning point, after which wages rise.
chains.result: The model makes development a structural change — labour moving from low- to high-productivity work. Whether it happens depends on reinvested profits, labour-intensive industry and jobs arriving as fast as migrants.

chains.title: A buffer stock through a good and a bad year
steps: The band for coffee is $2.00 to $2.40 a kilogram.
A bumper harvest of 480 thousand tonnes would push the price to $1.60.
The agency buys 80 thousand tonnes, holding the price at $2.00.
A poor harvest of 300 thousand tonnes would push it to $2.50.
The agency sells 20 thousand tonnes from store, holding it at $2.40.
chains.result: Farm incomes are steadier than the harvests. The scheme lasts only while good years and bad years roughly balance; a run of bumper harvests leaves the agency buying until its money runs out.

evaluation.title: Market-orientated or interventionist?
evaluation.content: Neither list wins in general, and an answer that declares one correct has missed the point. **Each strategy answers a constraint, and each needs conditions to work.** Market-orientated strategies raise efficiency and draw in foreign savings where markets function; interventionist strategies fill gaps where markets are missing, but need money, reserves and capable, honest administration. The strongest judgements name the constraint that binds hardest in the country in question — savings, foreign currency, skills, infrastructure or governance — and choose the strategy that relaxes it.

evaluation.title: Does the source of growth matter for development?
evaluation.content: Growth from a mine and growth from schools and small firms can raise GDP by the same amount and change lives very differently. **Ask who receives the income, what it is spent on, and whether it lasts.** Growth concentrated in a capital-intensive sector with few jobs may leave health and schooling unchanged; growth that raises output per worker across many people usually improves them. Growth can also carry environmental costs — pollution, lost forests, degraded land — which are a cost of economic growth in topic 2.3.5 and a reason to weigh how growth is achieved, not only how fast.

evaluation.title: Aid, debt relief and the institutions: help or dependency?
evaluation.content: The evidence depends on the type of help. **Humanitarian aid and health programmes have clear effects; large transfers to weak governments have much weaker ones.** Debt relief frees foreign currency and revenue but can reward overborrowing; IMF loans restore stability at the cost of conditions that can cut health and education spending; NGOs reach the poorest but at small scale. A strong evaluation asks what the money is spent on, who controls it, and whether it builds the capacity to grow without it.
